newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Bank of France cuts key interest rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of France cuts key interest rate.

text.p: The Bank of France trimmed a key interest rate on Thursday, lowering its intervention rate to 3.10 percent from 3.15 in a move whose timing largely surprised financial markets.

The move was announced after a meeting of the central bank's monetary policy council and surprised most economists who said earlier this week that the recent rise in the dollar had lowered the chances of a rate cut.
Economists said the urgency of short-term interest rate cuts had been reduced by the dollar rally against the franc and the mark because it could boost European growth.
Nevertheless, most said the independent central bank would gradually bring the intervention rate down to the level of the German repo rate, currently at three percent.
The Bank has traditionally maintained a small premium over the German repo rate to cushion the franc against any speculative attack on currency markets.
But financial markets expect the German and French interest rates to converge ahead of the locking of currency parities in European monetary union, due in January 1999.
"I didn't think they'd do it this week," said Jean-Louis Mourier, economist at Louis Dreyfus Finance. "The market was not convinced either, which explains the rise in PIBOR."
"This is no longer for the sake of the economy, it's all about convergence for EMU, for afterwards," Mourier added.
PIBOR interest rate futures jumped after the rate news, with the March contract climbing to 96.76, up six basis points. It was three basis point up just before the rate cut announcement.
The stability of the franc against the mark opened the door for a small interest rate cut, economists say.
The franc was trading at 3.3752 to the mark at 1300 GMT, nearly unchanged from its level before the Bank announced the cut.
The level is just short of its European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) central rate of 3.35, which some argue should be used as the basis for fixing parities in monetary union.

The move was likely to revive speculation that the appointment earlier this month of two new members to the nine-member monetary policy council, who are seen as close to President Jacques Chirac, has changed the Bank's traditionally cautious policy.
The intervention rate was last cut from 3.20 percent, on December 17. The Bank left the five-to-10 day rate, which is considered less important at the moment, unchanged at 4.60 percent.
